Capture energy from the sun and convert it into electricity. However, this is science, not magic. Solar panels use a curious scientific technique called the photovoltaic effect to convert one form of energy into another. Here's how solar panels harvest light and turn it into electricity. The sun is a mighty power, with an annual output of one billion (that is, one, then 34 zeros) joules. That's a lot. The whole planet is bathed in this flush of energy, which is one of the things that makes this so livable. It drives the weather, heats the atmosphere and makes life possible. So, is it useful to convert some of that energy into something we can use?
This is what plants do through photosynthesis, using light to bind carbon from the atmosphere to sugars that they metabolize and grow. The solar panels you're seeing on more and more rooftops do something similar, converting light into electricity. They can do this because of the so-called photovoltaic effect, which converts solar energy into electricity. Here's how it works: Sometimes, when light hits an atom, it gets absorbed by an electron around the atom, boosting the electron's energy. In some materials, such as some metals and silicon, this extra energy is enough to cause electrons to free atoms, allowing them to move within the material's crystal structure. If you create two crystal layers, you can use it.
One layer, called n-type material, is contaminated with a chemical (scientists call it a stimulant), meaning it has a lot of electrons, so it has extra electrons. The other layer is contaminated with another material that makes it want to absorb more electrons, called a P-type material. These electrons do not easily jump over the junction of the two materials (called an NP junction), so there is a voltage difference between the two layers. If you then connect the circuit to each side of this panel, this voltage can be used to power the device or charge the battery. Each solar cell generates only a small voltage, typically about 0.5V. The amount of current created depends on the size of the cell. This voltage can be increased if multiple batteries are connected together. So if you connect solar cells together to cover your roof, you could get enough electricity to power most of your house. Solar panels also generate direct current, rather than the alternating current provided by utilities. This means that the energy from the solar panels must be converted before it can drive the toaster. It also often requires storage: you might want to bake bread when the sun is down, and solar panels don't generate electricity in the dark.

The sun's energy can be converted into useful electricity in several ways. The two main methods are through photovoltaics (solar cells) and the concentration of solar power, but there are also numerous experimental technologies that are on the verge of becoming commercially applicable.
Photovoltaic (PV) technology is the use of solar cells to convert the sun's light into direct current using the photoelectric effect. This effect is the phenomenon in which electrons are emitted from matter after the absorption of electromagnetic radiation such as x-rays or visible light. When sunlight hits the solar panel, light is absorbed by the silicon and electrons are knocked loose from their atoms, allowing them to flow freely through the silicon to produce electricity.
PV panels contain an interconnected assembly of PV cells, also called solar cells. An installation on a rooftop or as a ground-mounted collection system is called a photovoltaic array and consists of multiple PV panels. Each cell on a panel is wired to connect to other cells and each panel is wired to connect to the other panels in an array. The array contains multiple panels, an inverter (which converts direct current to alternating current) and interconnection wiring to connect the system to the power grid.
PV has numerous applications from powering a calculator with a single solar cell, to powering off-grid homes with a few PV panels, to commercial-scale photovoltaic arrays composed of many connected solar panels.

Introduction
In the vast expanse of renewable energy, solar panels stand as the vanguards, capturing the sun's radiant energy and transforming it into electrical power. The key to this remarkable feat lies within the heart of solar panels — silicon. In this exploration, we not only unveil the reasons behind silicon's prominence in solar technology but also delve into the crucial role of the P-N-P junction, an intrinsic part of its functionality in photovoltaic cells.
The Pioneering Role of Silicon in Solar Panels
Silicon: A Sunlit Conductor
Abundance and Availability:
Silicon, constituting a significant portion of the Earth's crust, is the second most abundant element. Its widespread availability ensures the scalability and affordability of solar energy.
Semiconductor Properties:
Silicon's unique semiconductor properties make it an ideal material for converting sunlight into electrical energy. When exposed to sunlight, it generates an electric current through the photovoltaic effect.
At the core of a solar panel is the photovoltaic cell, where the photovoltaic effect takes place. When sunlight strikes the atoms within the cell, electrons are set into motion, creating an electric current.
The arrangement of atoms and their behavior under sunlight allows for the efficient generation of electricity, making silicon an ideal semiconductor material.
Types of Solar Cells
Crystalline Silicon Cells:
Monocrystalline Cells:
Comprising single crystal structures, monocrystalline silicon cells exhibit high efficiency. The uniformity of the crystal lattice allows for a more efficient conversion of sunlight into electricity.
Thin film solar cells use thin layers of semiconductor material. Although less efficient than crystalline silicon cells, thin film technology offers advantages in flexibility and lower manufacturing costs.
Silicon's Bandgap and the Spectrum of Sunlight
Adaptability to Sunlight:
Silicon's bandgap, the energy range where electrons are most efficiently excited, aligns well with the spectrum of sunlight. This adaptability allows solar cells to capture a broad range of sunlight wavelengths.
Harnessing sunlight across various wavelengths enhances the overall efficiency and performance of silicon-based solar panels.
The P-N-P Junction: Silicon's Intricate Dance
Formation of P-N-P Junction:
The P-N-P junction is a crucial element in the functionality of silicon solar cells. It is formed by introducing specific impurities into the silicon, creating regions with excess electrons (N-type) and regions with electron deficiencies (P-type).
The junction between these regions is the P-N-P junction, creating an electric field within the silicon.
Working of the P-N-P Junction:
When sunlight strikes the silicon at the P-N-P junction, it releases energy, allowing electrons to move across the junction.
The electric field within the P-N-P junction facilitates the separation of these electrons and creates a flow of electric current, contributing to the generation of electrical energy.
Solar Panels: A Symphony of Efficiency
High Efficiency of Crystalline Panels:
The crystalline structure of silicon cells, whether monocrystalline or polycrystalline, contributes to their high efficiency. Monocrystalline cells, with their uniform structure, exhibit particularly impressive efficiency levels.

Why do solar panels need a pn junction to make electricity?

What happens at pn junction in solar cell?

Why do we need a pn junction?

Is photovoltaic the same as solar?

How is photovoltaic energy generated?

What is MPPT in solar inverter?
MPPT stands for Maximum Power Point Tracker. It is a circuit (typically a DC to DC converter) employed in the majority of modern photovoltaic inverters. Its function is to maximize the energy available from the connected solar module arrays at any time during its operation.
